content: Hi, thanks so much for taking the time to chat today. I'm looking forward to hearing about the VUB Publications Management System and how it can best support your needs. The way this will go is pretty simple: I'll ask you some questions, but feel free to pause or ask me to clarify anything at any point. To get started, could you describe the project context and the problem the system should address from your perspective?

At VUB we need one central place to manage publication records and the actual full texts behind them, because right now that information is spread across different sources and is hard to keep consistent. The main problem is making sure researchers and staff can find, upload, correct, and validate publication data without duplicating work or losing control over quality. We also want the system to help us extract metadata from documents and deal with variations in author or institution names so the records stay coherent over time.

You mentioned the need to keep publication data consistent and avoid duplication, which sounds like a key goal. Could you share what the main goals or success criteria for the Publications Management System are from your perspective? For example, what would make this system a clear success for VUB?

A clear success would be that staff can enter or import publications once and then reuse that information reliably across the university, with much less manual cleanup. It should noticeably improve the quality and completeness of the publication repository, especially by reducing duplicates, missing metadata, and inconsistent names. If users can quickly find the right record, upload the full text, and have moderators approve changes without creating bottlenecks, that would also be a strong sign it is working well.

That makes a lot of sense, especially the part about reducing duplicates and avoiding bottlenecks. To get a clearer picture, could you share if there are any specific measurable outcomes or key performance indicators you’d like to see improved once the system is in place? For example, targets around how much faster publications can be found, or how much duplication should be reduced, or any quality metrics you have in mind?

We do not have hard targets agreed yet, so I can’t give you exact percentages. In practice, we would want to see fewer duplicate records, fewer corrections needed after import, and a much shorter turnaround time for moderation and publication approval. It would also be useful to track how many records arrive with complete bibliographic metadata on the first pass, because that tells us whether the extraction and import workflows are actually helping.

Thanks for sharing those practical outcomes you’re aiming for. To get a clearer picture of how the system will support everyone involved, could you walk me through the different user roles you expect in the Publications Management System? For example, who will be uploading publications, who will be moderating or approving changes, and are there other distinct roles we should keep in mind?

We definitely expect different roles with different access rights, because not everyone should be able to do everything. In broad terms, researchers or staff will upload and edit their own publications, while a central team or moderator group will review, correct, and approve records before they become authoritative. I also expect administrators to manage permissions and system settings, but the exact role structure is something we may still need to confirm internally.

That's helpful to know about the broad roles. To get a clearer picture, could you describe the different user groups who will interact with the Publications Management System and what their main responsibilities or roles will be?

The main groups are researchers, departmental or faculty staff, central library or repository staff, and system administrators. Researchers will usually submit publications and full texts, while staff may help clean up metadata, import batches, and handle corrections for their units. The central repository team will moderate and validate records, and administrators will take care of user access and configuration.

Thanks for outlining those user groups and their responsibilities. To get a better sense of how the system will support their day-to-day work, could you walk me through the typical business events or workflows these groups follow when managing publication data? For example, what steps happen from the moment a publication is uploaded, through any corrections, to final approval?

A typical workflow starts when a user uploads a publication file or enters a record manually, and the system tries to extract the bibliographic details automatically. After that, the record is checked for completeness and possible duplicates, and if needed someone corrects the metadata or reconciles the author and institution names. Once the record is satisfactory, it goes to moderation for approval, and then it becomes available as an authoritative publication record with the full text linked or stored if that is permitted.

You gave a great overview of the workflow. To help us design the system’s data handling better, are there any specific terms, naming conventions, or domain-specific concepts related to publications, authors, or institutions that the system should understand or handle carefully to keep data consistent and accurate?

Yes, the system should handle variant names very carefully, especially for authors and institutions, because the same person or organization can appear under different spellings or formats. We also need it to distinguish between the bibliographic record itself and the full text or file attached to it, since those are related but not the same thing. Beyond that, I would say publication types, affiliation data, and identifiers like ISBN, ISSN, DOI, or ORCID are important concepts to treat consistently.

Building on what you shared about variant names and key identifiers, could you describe any specific domain terminology or jargon used within VUB or the Publications Management System context that we should be aware of to ensure shared understanding across all user groups?

A few terms come up a lot internally, like “bibliographic record,” “full text,” “metadata,” and “authority record” for the standardized version of an author or institution name. People also talk about “deposit” or “submission” when they mean uploading a publication, and “moderation” when the central team reviews it before approval. I think those terms are fairly standard, but there may be local VUB-specific shorthand that we would need to confirm with the repository team.

Thanks for clarifying those key terms — that really helps set the stage. To get a clearer picture of how things flow day-to-day, could you walk me through the detailed business events or workflows that happen from the moment a publication is uploaded until it’s fully approved and published? I’m especially interested in any decision points or handoffs between user roles along the way.

It usually starts with a researcher or staff member depositing a file or entering the publication manually, and then the system captures whatever metadata it can from the document. If the record looks incomplete, has conflicting information, or matches an existing publication, it goes back to the submitter or to a metadata editor for correction and consolidation. After that, the central moderation team checks the record, confirms the author and institution links, and approves it so the publication is published in the system and available for search and download according to the access rules.

You mentioned that records with incomplete or conflicting information get sent back for correction, which is great. Could you share more about the kinds of exceptions or unusual cases the system might encounter—like conflicting metadata, failed imports, or unusual publication types—and how you’d like the system to handle those situations?

We do expect cases where the metadata extraction is wrong or incomplete, especially from scanned PDFs or older documents, so the system should flag those clearly rather than quietly accepting them. Failed imports or duplicate records should be logged and made visible to the relevant user so they can fix the problem or retry the import. For unusual publication types, I’d expect the system to allow some flexibility, but if it cannot classify something confidently, it should leave it for manual review instead of forcing a bad choice.

You’ve given a helpful overview of how the system should flag and log issues like incomplete metadata or duplicates. Could you walk me through what happens next in those cases? For example, which user roles get involved to resolve these exceptions, and what steps or workflows they follow to fix or approve the records before they can move forward?

In most cases, the first response would be by the person who uploaded the record or by a departmental editor, since they know the publication best and can correct obvious mistakes. If the issue is about duplicate authors, institution names, or more general metadata quality, it usually moves to the central repository or library team for reconciliation and validation. Once they are satisfied that the record is clean and complete, they approve it and it can continue into the normal published state.

Thanks for explaining the roles involved in fixing issues. Could you describe in more detail how the system should handle situations like failed metadata extraction, conflicting information, or uncertain duplicate detection? For example, how should these exceptions be flagged, logged, and made visible to users, and what steps or options should users have to resolve or retry these cases?

The system should make those cases very visible in the record, with a clear status like incomplete, needs review, or duplicate suspected, so users immediately see that something is wrong. It should keep an audit trail of what failed, what data was extracted, and who changed it, because we need traceability when a record is corrected later. Users should be able to edit the metadata, retry the import or extraction if the source file changes, and either confirm or reject a suspected duplicate, but anything still uncertain should stay in a review queue until someone with the right authority resolves it.

To get a better sense of how the Publications Management System fits into the bigger picture, could you describe any external systems or services it will need to connect with? For example, are there bibliographic databases, institutional systems, or author identifier services it should exchange data with? What kind of data or functionality would you expect from those interactions?

Yes, it should connect to some source systems where publication data may already exist, like institutional research information systems or library catalog data if that is available. It would also be useful to exchange data with identifier services such as ORCID for authors and possibly DOI-related services for publication metadata validation. In those cases, I would expect the system to import and update core bibliographic fields, author affiliations, identifiers, and maybe status information, but I don’t know yet which specific external platforms VUB has already approved.

That makes sense, thanks for outlining those key external sources. Could you describe in a bit more detail which specific external systems or interfaces the Publications Management System should connect with? For example, are there particular institutional repositories, bibliographic databases, or author identifier services you expect to integrate with? Also, what kinds of data or functionality should these integrations support—like automatic updates, validation checks, or synchronization of author and publication details?

I know ORCID is definitely relevant for author identification, and DOI/Crossref-style lookup would make sense for validating publication metadata. On the institutional side, there may be a connection to the university’s research information or repository environment, but I can’t name the exact system without checking with the team. The main functions I’d expect are import of metadata, validation of titles and identifiers, and occasional synchronization of author and publication details, rather than fully automatic two-way updating for everything.

You’ve mentioned ORCID and DOI/Crossref as important external services, and possibly a connection to the university’s research information system. Could you share if there are any other specific external systems or interfaces the Publications Management System should connect with? For example, institutional repositories, library catalogs, or authentication providers? Also, what kinds of data or functionality would you expect these integrations to support—like importing existing records, validating metadata, synchronizing author details, or something else?

Besides ORCID and DOI lookup, I would expect some form of institutional authentication, probably tied to the university’s login environment, so users can act according to their roles. A connection to the library or repository side would also be useful for importing existing records and avoiding duplicate work, but I’m not sure yet whether that is a direct system integration or a file-based exchange. In general, these integrations should support importing and validating bibliographic data, matching authors and affiliations, and updating records when there is trusted external information, but not blindly overwriting local corrections.

You’ve shared some great points about the external systems and data exchanges. To help us plan the project well, are there any specific constraints or rules around these integrations? For example, do you have preferences or requirements on how often data should be updated, which sources are trusted, or how the system should handle conflicts between external data and local corrections?

We would want trusted sources to be clearly prioritized, so institutional data and identifier services like ORCID should usually win over unverified manual input, but local corrections should not be overwritten without review. I don’t think everything needs real-time updates; for most records, scheduled sync or on-demand lookup would be enough, as long as the system shows when the external data was last checked. If there is a conflict, the safest approach is to flag it for human review and keep both the external value and the local value visible until someone decides.

Thanks for clarifying the data update and conflict handling approach. Shifting gears a bit, could you describe how you envision the Publications Management System integrating with the university’s institutional authentication? For example, how should it enforce user roles and permissions based on that integration, and what role-based access controls would be important to support within the system?

It should use the university login so people come in with their existing identity, and the system then maps that identity to a role like author, departmental editor, librarian, or administrator. Those roles should control what they can see and do, especially around uploading, editing, approving, moderating, and managing duplicates or institutional names. I’d also expect some restrictions so users only modify records they own or are responsible for, while central staff can work across the full dataset.

Could you describe in more detail the kinds of permissions and restrictions each user role should have? For example, what actions should authors be able to perform versus departmental editors or moderators? Are there any special cases or exceptions we should be aware of when enforcing these roles?

Authors should be able to upload their own publications, correct metadata for their own records, and view the status of items they submitted. Departmental editors would handle records for their unit, so they should be able to review, edit, and submit records for approval, but not make broad system changes. Moderators or library staff should have the final say on conflicts, duplicates, and name reconciliation, and administrators would manage roles and system settings; the main exception is when a record is shared across units, because then ownership and edit rights can overlap and need to be handled carefully.

Thanks for clarifying the roles and their permissions. Shifting focus a bit, could you share if there are any legal, standards, or compliance obligations the Publications Management System must meet when exchanging data with external services like ORCID or DOI providers? For example, are there specific data privacy, licensing, or metadata standards that the system should adhere to?

Yes, we would need to be careful with GDPR and general data minimization, especially when exchanging personal data like author identifiers, affiliations, or contact details. I would also expect the system to respect whatever licensing or reuse terms apply to imported metadata, and to store provenance so we know where each piece of data came from. As for standards, using common bibliographic formats and identifier standards is important, but I’d need to verify exactly which ones VUB wants to mandate.

Building on what you shared about legal and compliance needs, are there particular operational quality attributes—like security, privacy, capacity, scalability, availability, reliability, or fault tolerance—that you consider especially important for the Publications Management System? Could you share any examples or scenarios that illustrate these needs or challenges you want to avoid?

Security and privacy are definitely top priorities because the system will hold personal and publication data, and not everyone should see or change everything. Availability is also important during busy periods, like when researchers are preparing annual reporting or uploading many publications at once, so the system should not become a bottleneck. I’d also want it to be reliable with imports and bulk processing, because partial failures or silent data corruption would be a serious problem we want to avoid.

You’ve highlighted security, privacy, availability, and reliability really well. To round out our understanding of operational qualities, could you share your thoughts on capacity, scalability, and fault tolerance? For example, how many publications or users should the system handle smoothly, and what kinds of failures or load spikes should it be prepared for without losing data or performance?

I don’t have exact numbers yet, but it should comfortably handle the full university publication backlog plus ongoing yearly growth without slowing down noticeably for normal use. The bigger concern is bursty activity, like large imports, end-of-year updates, or many users searching and editing at the same time, so it should scale reasonably in those moments. For fault tolerance, I would expect it to recover cleanly from failed imports or interrupted sessions without losing already saved records, and any unfinished processing should be resumable or at least clearly flagged.

Building on what you shared about capacity and fault tolerance, could you share any specific examples or scenarios where availability or reliability issues caused problems in your current setup, or that you particularly want to avoid in the Publications Management System? Understanding these will help us prioritize critical operational needs.

The main thing we want to avoid is losing work when someone spends time cleaning up a record and the session times out or the import process fails halfway through. Another common pain point is when metadata changes don’t propagate clearly, so users think a publication is updated but older values still appear in reports or search results. We also want to avoid long outages during peak reporting periods, because that would create a lot of manual work and frustration for the teams using the system.

You’ve mentioned security and privacy as top priorities earlier, which makes a lot of sense given the sensitive data involved. Could you share some specific examples or scenarios where security or privacy concerns have impacted your current processes or where you want the new system to be especially strong? For instance, are there particular risks or challenges you want to avoid around unauthorized access, data leaks, or managing sensitive author information?

We want to avoid situations where someone can see or edit records outside their department, or where draft metadata becomes visible before it is approved. Another concern is exposing personal data more widely than necessary, especially author identifiers and any internal notes about record quality or conflicts. It would also be important to log who changed what, so we can trace unexpected edits and investigate if something looks wrong.

You mentioned the importance of restricting access and logging changes, which makes a lot of sense. Building on that, could you elaborate on how the system should handle situations where publication records are shared across multiple departments or units? For example, how should overlapping ownership and edit rights be managed to avoid conflicts or confusion when several users have permission to edit the same record?

In shared cases, I’d expect one record to have a clear primary owner, even if other departments can also propose changes. A good approach would be that one unit can approve final edits, while the others can suggest corrections or comment, so we avoid people overwriting each other. If two groups disagree on a record, the moderator should resolve it and the system should keep a history of the competing changes.

That makes a lot of sense to have a clear primary owner with others able to suggest changes and a moderator resolving conflicts. Could you share an example from your current setup where overlapping ownership of a publication record caused challenges? How do you imagine the new system could help coordinate edits or resolve conflicts in such situations?

A typical issue is when a publication is relevant to both a faculty and a research group, and each side updates different fields without telling the other, so the record ends up inconsistent. Sometimes one team corrects a title or author list while another later overwrites part of that work because they assumed they owned the whole record. The new system should make ownership and pending changes visible, and ideally warn users when someone else has edited the same record recently so they can coordinate before saving.

Thanks for that clear example—it really helps to understand the challenges. Could you describe in more detail how you envision the governance model working for these shared publication records? For instance, how should proposal rights, approvals, and moderator conflict resolution be structured to keep things smooth and transparent? Are there particular workflows or rules you’d want the system to enforce around this?

I think proposal rights should be fairly broad for the people linked to the record, but final approval should stay with a smaller trusted group, probably the primary owner plus designated moderators. The system should keep proposed changes separate from the published version until they are approved, and it should show who proposed what and when. For conflicts, I’d want a simple rule that the latest proposal does not overwrite anything automatically; instead, moderators compare the versions, choose what to keep, and leave a note explaining the decision.

You’ve outlined a clear governance model for proposals and approvals, which is great. Building on that, how do you imagine the system should present ownership, pending changes, and recent edits to users? For example, what kind of visibility or warnings would help users coordinate better and avoid accidentally overwriting each other’s work?

It should be very visible on the record page who is the primary owner, who else has editing rights, and whether there are any pending proposals waiting for approval. I’d also want a clear “last edited by” and “last edited at” indicator, plus a warning if someone else has changed the record since the user opened it. If possible, the system should make users explicitly confirm when they are about to overwrite a more recent version, so accidental conflicts are less likely.

We’ve covered a lot about governance and collaboration so far, which is great. Shifting gears a bit, could you share your expectations or any concerns regarding how easy the Publications Management System should be for new users to learn and get up to speed? Are there particular challenges you foresee around training or onboarding that we should keep in mind?

It should be fairly easy to pick up, because we’ll have occasional users as well as people who work with it every day. The main concern is that if the workflow for importing, correcting, and approving records is too complicated, people will make mistakes or rely on the wrong shortcuts. So I’d want the interface to guide users step by step and make the most common actions obvious without needing a lot of training.

You mentioned the importance of making the system easy to learn and guiding users through common actions. Building on that, how important is accessibility for your diverse user base? Are there particular accessibility standards or specific user groups we should keep in mind to ensure everyone can use the system comfortably?

Accessibility is important, yes, because we have a mixed user base and not everyone works the same way or has the same level of technical comfort. I don’t know if we have a formal standard already mandated, but it would be safest to aim for a widely recognized public-sector accessibility level, and to make sure the interface works well with keyboard navigation and screen readers. We should also keep in mind users who may need clearer contrast, simpler language, or fewer steps when handling routine tasks.

Since accessibility is important and you have a diverse user base, I’m curious how you envision the system supporting users during the transition from your current scattered setup to this new centralized Publications Management System. Specifically, what would make migrating existing publication data and user workflows smoother for your teams? Are there particular challenges or expectations around data migration or product migration that we should keep in mind to help users adapt comfortably?

The migration should be as automatic as possible, especially for existing bibliographic data and file attachments, because manual cleanup for everything would be too heavy. I’d expect some imported records to be messy or incomplete, so the system should flag duplicates, missing metadata, and uncertain author names for review instead of forcing a perfect import on day one. For the users, it would help a lot if the new system feels close to the current workflow for the basic tasks, with training and a phased rollout so people can adapt gradually.

That makes a lot of sense to keep the migration smooth and manageable. Could you share more about the data conversion process you expect? For example, what kinds of source data formats or systems will we need to handle, and are there particular challenges with legacy data—like inconsistent metadata or missing fields—that the system should be prepared to convert or clean up automatically?

We’ll likely need to handle data coming from spreadsheets, export files from older repository tools, and some directly from documents or PDFs. The biggest problems are usually inconsistent author names, missing DOI or ISSN values, and records where the same publication was entered more than once with slightly different metadata. I’d expect the system to normalize what it can, but still let a curator review anything uncertain rather than guessing silently.

Thanks for outlining the main data sources and challenges. Could you describe how you envision the system supporting the cleanup and normalization process during data conversion? For example, what kinds of automatic fixes or flags should it apply, and how would curators or users interact with those flagged records to review and resolve uncertainties?

It should do straightforward normalization automatically, like standardizing date formats, cleaning whitespace, unifying obvious duplicate fields, and matching known journal or institution names against controlled lists. When it sees something uncertain, like two possible author identities or a missing identifier, it should flag it clearly and explain why it was flagged. Curators should then be able to accept, edit, merge, or reject the suggested correction from a review queue rather than hunting through the imported records one by one.

Could you describe in detail the types of source data formats and legacy systems from which publication data will need to be migrated? What specific challenges do you anticipate with inconsistent or missing metadata during this conversion process?

We’ll probably see Excel sheets, CSV exports, older repository databases, and PDF or Word documents that were used as source material. Sometimes there are multiple internal systems in parallel, so the same publication can exist in slightly different versions across departments or institutes. The main challenges are inconsistent author spellings, missing identifiers like DOI or ORCID, incomplete affiliations, and metadata that was entered with different local conventions over time.

Thanks for sharing those details about the source formats and metadata challenges. Building on that, what are your expectations for how the system should flag and handle duplicates, missing metadata, or uncertain author and institution names during the migration? How would you like these flags to be presented to users to make review and correction as efficient and clear as possible?

I’d want duplicates to be grouped together with a clear suggestion of which record looks most complete, instead of just listing them separately. Missing metadata should be flagged by field, with the most important gaps made very visible, and uncertain names should show the possible matches so a curator can choose quickly. Ideally the user can resolve several issues from one screen, with a short explanation of why the system thinks something needs attention.

You’ve given a great picture of how the system should flag and group issues for review. Thinking about the people side of things, how do you envision supporting users during the transition to this new system and after migration? For example, what kinds of training, help, or ongoing support would make it easier for researchers, staff, and moderators to adapt and keep publication data accurate over time?

We’d need short training sessions tailored to different roles, because researchers, administrative staff, and moderators won’t use the system in the same way. A clear help section with examples for common tasks, plus a small set of contact people who can answer questions during the first months, would make the transition much smoother. After migration, I think periodic reminders about data quality and a simple way to report issues would help keep the records accurate without creating too much extra work.
